pi.name: Sara Aton
pi.title: Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology
pi.bio: Sara Aton received her PhD in Neuroscience from Washington University in St. Louis, where she worked with Erik Herzog, and completed postdoctoral training with Marcos Frank at the University of Pennsylvania. She joined the Department of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology at the University of Michigan as an Assistant Professor in 2012, was promoted to Associate Professor with tenure in 2019, and to Professor in 2024. Her research examines how sensory experience and sleep shape neural circuits, with a focus on the mechanisms underlying plasticity and memory formation.

description: The Aton Lab studies how neuronal and network activity during sleep and waking contributes to neural plasticity following novel sensory experiences. Using mice, the lab investigates how sleep supports two processes: hippocampal long-term memory formation and visual cortex plasticity. The group combines behavioral, biochemical, electrophysiological, and optogenetic techniques in freely behaving animals to link brain-state-specific network activity to the intracellular signaling and structural changes that consolidate memories. The lab also asks whether abnormal sleep contributes to cognitive deficits in neurodevelopmental disorders such as Fragile X syndrome, Angelman syndrome, and autism spectrum disorders.

areas.title: Thalamocortical oscillations and sleep-dependent plasticity
areas.summary: Tests whether high-amplitude, low-frequency oscillations during sleep uniquely promote cortical plasticity, using optogenetic tools to silence oscillation-generating neurons while recording neural activity and plasticity in freely behaving mice.

areas.title: Sleep and hippocampal memory consolidation
areas.summary: Explores how network activity during sleep activates intracellular signaling pathways needed to convert short-term memories into long-term memories, combining electrophysiology, optogenetics, and biochemistry.

areas.title: Sleep and neurodevelopmental disorders
areas.summary: Investigates whether abnormal sleep contributes to cognitive deficits in autism spectrum disorders, Fragile X syndrome, and Angelman syndrome, and how disease-associated mutations affect sleep behavior and the network activity associated with memory consolidation.

joining: The lab is actively seeking applications from undergraduate students for the Fall 2026 semester; interested students apply through a Qualtrics form linked from the Join Us page. The lab offers training in research methodology, involvement in research initiatives, and a collaborative team environment, and looks for research enthusiasm, reliable and precise work habits, and openness to learning. Contact Dr. Sara Aton (734-615-1576) or the lab (734-936-6864).
